Error Level Analysis –  These types of inconsistencies are produced by recompressing the image as a JPEG of quality 75 and subtracting the new image from the old. Median Noise Residuals – These type of inconsistencies are based on isolating the almost-invisible image noise through median filtering. Only similar regions are compared, i.e. edges are compared to edges, textures to textures, and uniform regions to uniform regions.

The Discrete Wavelet Noise algorithm filters the image and calculates the local noise distribution at each part of the image. Regions that differ from the rest of the image are highlighted in strong red, and are likely to originate from other images.

My family has been bee keepers since before I was born and this DIRECTLY affected our income. How? The first thing that alarmed the entire bee keeping industry and commercial honey production business was the importation of Chinese honey. First problem was the huge price disparity. China shipped over boat loads of this cheap honey. Next problem was that the honey was very low quality. It had a higher moisture content, was dark and had a nasty flavor. Then the honey packing plants who bought this cheap honey couldn't have it compete with domestic honey so they blended it with higher grade US honey which they sold as "Blended American Honey". Needless to say quality suffered as did honey sales and whole sale prices we received dropped. I can clearly remember this topic listening to adults talking about it. They were outraged. So, state beekeeping associations around the nation pooled funding to send in people to lobby on behalf of American Honey producers. No one listened. Instead, the politicians we appealed to mocked us with, "What, bees aren't communists!" "You think the little bees are commies? Hahahaha" China subsidized their beekeepers, shipped them around to the bee yards, provided spaces for bees, paid for the equipment and meanwhile their beekeepers lived like dogs, slept in bushes, ate old rice cakes and wore rags. We have to compete with that shit? Then we did testing to see what else was going on with this Chinese honey. We discovered that the Chinese were mixing corn syrup with the honey. It was adulterated honey. US honey has strict standards. To comply we can't have any adulterations. Before the honey flow starts we must stop all winter feeding and then be careful to not take honey stores from bottom levels where the syrup may be stored. Fortunately, this isn't hard to do as bees really don't mix feed syrup with new nectar. Nectar and honey are visually different, taste different and nectar stores always carry a floral aroma. BTW, you can't get that rich aroma from blended honey as it's heated until the natural aroma vanishes as it's a fragile component of the honey. After that, finding there was no political backlash our government allowed honey from Brazil as well. This honey is so full of moisture that it must be sold before production and shipped as soon as possible or it ferments in the drums. Even then, it also has to be cooked to remove the fermentation and alcohol. Then, also it's blended with American honey which happens to be the best in the world.

Since those days Chinese imports of every type have flooded the market with what the Chinese call, "Lucky Junk".

Remember the whole Killer Bee thing? What a farce. First, the government and the media went into fear mongering instead of actually educating the public. Killer bees are the same as regular domestic bees with one exception. They are more aggressive. Same bee, same species that is, but genetically adapted to be more aggressive. Like the difference between a pit bull and a Labrador.

As the Africanized bees came north from Brazil they mixed with more docile feral bees but not that much as the further south you go in the America's the less domestic honey bee culture there is. Into Mexico there is a large population of domestic and feral bees. The feral bees are not indigenous but are rather European Honey Bees that have escaped and gone feral. The Africanized Bees mixed readily with these populations as they spread north. By the time these bees got to our southern border they were largely hybridized. Neither fully Africanized lineage nor European honey bees. You could get a swarm that was more like Africanized bees or more like European honey bee.

So, here's the difference besides simply being more aggressive.

Africanized bees will indeed get more honey. But the problem is, they are adjusted to a hotter climate so they don't hibernate well. They will also take up and fly away if disturbed. The bees will just suck up as much honey as they can carry and fly away with their queen if she can fly. In addition, after you work the hive, the bees will remain aggressive up to five days or so after being disturbed and even when not disturbed they will attack up to 100 feet away. When working them, instead of just a few more aggressive bees coming out to sting, every bee that can fly will come out and mob you, trying like hell to sting you. So, all things considered, they don't make good domestic bees. The reason the one scientist imported them to Brazil was in the hopes of hybridizing them with European bees to produce a good mix of traits. Now, in my mind, this is just a misguided attempt. We already have very good strains of honey bees. See here: https://morningchores.com/breeds-of-honey-bees/ My Grandfather used almost exclusively Carniolan honey bees for their gentle nature, eagerness to forage for honey and so I learned how to work those hives and what problems to look for. Grandpa liked to order his queen bees from a producer and the queens would come in little cages ready to be placed into new hive divides. It was always a proud day to make the trip to the post office to pick up our package of queens. The people working at the post office were always amused and a bit excited about this special delivery and they would notify us when it arrived and always have us come to the back door after hours and then gingerly bring out our precious package of buzzing bees. We would take them home, break apart the package and then feed the little cages of queens with their retinue of about five or six attendants. The thing about all those queens close to each other is that it pisses them off. Each one is ready for a fight to the death with other queens she can hear and smell in the other cages. They will make little ZZZZZ ZZZZZZ ZZZZZ noises to signal a willingness to fight. It's the queen version of, "Bring it bitch!" "Right here bitch, I got this!". Now, if you just go out and split up a hive to make divisions, there are several ways to do it. I hated my Grandpa's method as it had a high rate of failure that only increased as he got older and began to lose his touch. I learned a method from the president of the California State Beekeeper's Association who I worked with a few times. He took me out and gave me direct on hands instruction. His method was to completely separate the new division from the parent hive. My family would have us find and isolate the queen and then make divides. This man reasoned with me, "Why do you need to find the queen? Just make sure you DON'T have her and continue the division. Instead of placing the division back on top of the parent hive with a board separating them, complete the divide and place on a new bottom board. Then place your queen cage and leave it. Don't disturb it for a week". My Grandpa toward the end of his career was losing up to half his queens with his methods. Following this man's instruction I was getting 95 percent take at very worst and approaching 99 percent.

But, I digress. Today, most feral bees in swarms are highly likely to have some bit of Africanized honey bee in their genetic makeup so with feral or captured bees, you just don't know what you can get or what to expect. You can have a flighty hive that will swarm out and abandon the nest at the first sign of disturbance or hives that don't get honey very well. Or, you may luck out, the bees stay and produce but are vicious. Or, produce and are docile. For a hobbyist, taking chances is all part of the fun and games. For commercial producers, they like to know how their bees are going to behave so they often tend to just order queens from a producer who they can trust to deliver as promised.

One more thing about Africanized bees that most people aren't aware of. Their stingers are about a third longer than European bees. In other words, the stingers can penetrate leather gloves if the gloves are too thin and the stingers can penetrate coveralls. They will also mob the worker unless the worker uses heavy smoke to confuse the attack. Moving such bees in the evening we took to leaving at least one beehive behind to collect those who had refused to go in at dusk. Africanized bees seemed to form clouds of angry bees when we were moving them and after loading up they would collect on the last hives until it was just a pillar of bees. You couldn't even see the bee hives except for a corner sticking out.

She did well then. I like to pack new foundation combs next to the transplanted combs if there's a honey flow going on. When the new combs get drawn out a bit they can be carefully pulled and inspected for eggs. If you see a regular pattern of fresh eggs in the center of the comb with only one regularly positioned eggs per cell it's confirmed you have a functioning queen. Just gently replace the newly drawn out comb and leave them alone. If there's no more eggs to be seen in any comb no matter how carefully you inspect with the sun behind your shoulder, then you don't have a queen and the hive will die out.
